title: LRU Cache
description:
Problem

Design and implement a Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache. It should support get and put operations in O(1) time.

Functional Requirements
  • get(key) — Return the value if the key exists, otherwise return -1. Accessing a key marks it as recently used.
  • put(key, value) — Insert or update the key-value pair. If the cache is at capacity, evict the least recently used entry before inserting.
Non-Functional Requirements
  • Both operations must run in O(1) time
  • Capacity is fixed at construction time

Example

val cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put(1, 1)
cache.put(2, 2)
cache.get(1)    // → 1  (1 is now most recent)
cache.put(3, 3) // evicts key 2
cache.get(2)    // → -1 (evicted)
cache.get(3)    // → 3
hints: What data structure gives you O(1) lookup by key?
To track recency, you need to know both the most recent and least recent entries quickly. A doubly linked list lets you remove and add nodes in O(1) — combine it with a HashMap.
Use a HashMap<Int, Node> where each Node is in a doubly linked list. On every get/put, move that node to the head (most recent). The tail is always the LRU candidate to evict.
approach:
Data Structure

Use a HashMap + Doubly Linked List. The map gives O(1) access to any node. The linked list maintains recency order — head is most recent, tail is least recent.

Key Operations

  • get: Look up node in map → move to head → return value
  • put: If key exists, update + move to head. If new, add at head. If over capacity, remove tail node and its map entry.
What most candidates miss
  • Using LinkedHashMap shortcut — fine for production but expect a "implement from scratch" follow-up
  • Forgetting to update the map when evicting the tail node
  • Off-by-one: checking capacity before insertion vs after
summary: Implement an LRU cache in Kotlin with O(1) get and put. Android machine coding interview question with hints, tests and a reference solution.

title: Token Bucket Rate Limiter
description:
Problem

Implement a Token Bucket Rate Limiter that controls how many requests each user can make per second.

Functional Requirements
  • isAllowed(userId) — Return true if the request is permitted, false if rate limited
  • Each user gets their own independent bucket
  • Bucket refills at a fixed rate over time (not just at fixed intervals)
  • Bucket has a max capacity — tokens don't accumulate beyond it
Token Bucket Rules
  • Each request consumes 1 token
  • Tokens refill continuously at refillRatePerSecond
  • If bucket is empty → request is denied
  • Users start with a full bucket
hints: You don't need an actual background thread to refill tokens. How can you calculate how many tokens should have been added since the last request, using only the current timestamp?
Store the last-access timestamp per user. On each request, compute elapsed time → multiply by refill rate → add tokens (capped at maxTokens).
Use a data class to hold each user's current token count and last refill timestamp. Use System.currentTimeMillis() for time tracking.
approach:
Lazy Refill Strategy

Don't use a background thread. Instead, calculate tokens lazily: on each request, check how much time has elapsed since the last request for that user, compute how many tokens should have been added, and top up the bucket.

Per-user State

data class Bucket(
  var tokens: Double,
  var lastRefillTime: Long
)
What most candidates miss
  • Using integer tokens instead of Double — causes precision loss with fractional refill rates
  • Not capping tokens at maxTokens after refill
  • Thread safety — a real implementation needs synchronization per user bucket
summary: Build a per-user token bucket rate limiter in Kotlin with lazy refill. Android machine coding question with hints, tests and a solution.

title: Event Bus
description:
Problem

Implement a publish-subscribe Event Bus that allows components to communicate without direct references to each other.

Functional Requirements
  • subscribe(eventType, listener) — Register a listener for an event type. Returns a unique subscriptionId.
  • unsubscribe(subscriptionId) — Remove a specific subscription
  • publish(eventType, data) — Notify all active listeners for that event type
  • Multiple listeners can subscribe to the same event type
  • Unsubscribing one listener should not affect others
hints: What data structure lets you look up all listeners for a given event type instantly?
Use a Map<String, Map<String, Listener>> — outer key is eventType, inner key is subscriptionId. This gives O(1) subscribe, unsubscribe, and publish.
For subscriptionId, use a UUID or a simple incrementing counter. Store a reverse mapping (subscriptionId → eventType) so unsubscribe doesn't need to scan all event types.
approach:
Data Structure

Use two maps: listeners: Map<EventType, Map<SubId, Listener>> and subscriptionIndex: Map<SubId, EventType>. The second map makes unsubscribe O(1) without scanning.

What most candidates miss
  • ConcurrentModificationException — if a listener modifies subscriptions during publish, iterate a copy
  • Memory leaks — not cleaning up empty event type entries after all listeners unsubscribe
  • Not handling the case where unsubscribe is called with an invalid ID
summary: Implement a publish-subscribe event bus in Kotlin: subscribe, unsubscribe, publish. Android machine coding question with tests and a solution.

title: Pagination Manager
description:
Problem

Implement a Pagination Manager that splits a dataset into pages and supports navigation.

Functional Requirements
  • getPage(pageNumber) — Return the correct slice of items for that page (1-indexed)
  • nextPage(current) — Return the next page or null if on last page
  • previousPage(current) — Return the previous page or null if on first page
  • Each Page object carries: items, currentPage, totalPages, hasNext, hasPrevious
  • Page numbers outside 1..totalPages throw IllegalArgumentException

Example

// 23 items, pageSize = 5 → 5 pages
// Page 1: [1,2,3,4,5]
// Page 5: [21,22,23]  ← last page may be smaller
hints: Total pages = ceil(totalItems / pageSize). Use integer math: (totalItems + pageSize - 1) / pageSize
For page N, the start index is (N-1) * pageSize. The end index is min(startIndex + pageSize, totalItems).
Validate pageNumber bounds — throw or return an empty page for out-of-range requests.
approach:
Index Calculation

Page N (1-indexed): startIndex = (pageNumber - 1) * pageSize, endIndex = min(startIndex + pageSize, items.size). Total pages: ceil(items.size / pageSize.toFloat()).toInt().

What most candidates miss
  • Off-by-one on the last page when items don't divide evenly
  • Not validating out-of-bounds page numbers
  • Using 0-indexed pages when the spec says 1-indexed
summary: Write a pagination manager in Kotlin: pages, navigation and bounds checks. Android machine coding question with hints, tests and a solution.

title: Retry with Exponential Backoff
description:
Problem

Implement a retry mechanism with exponential backoff that wraps any suspending function and retries it automatically on failure.

Functional Requirements
  • Retry up to maxAttempts times on exception
  • Delay between retries grows exponentially: initialDelay × multiplier^attempt
  • Cap delay at maxDelayMs to avoid unbounded waits
  • If all attempts fail, throw the last exception
  • If an attempt succeeds, return the result immediately
Delay Schedule (example)
  • Attempt 1 fails → wait 100ms
  • Attempt 2 fails → wait 200ms
  • Attempt 3 fails → wait 400ms (or maxDelay, whichever is lower)
hints: Use a loop from 1 to maxAttempts. Wrap each attempt in try-catch.
Track the current delay. After each failure (except the last), call delay(currentDelay) then multiply currentDelay by the multiplier. Use minOf(currentDelay, maxDelayMs) to cap it.
The function signature should be generic: suspend fun <T> retryWithBackoff(..., block: suspend () -> T): T. Rethrow on last attempt by checking attempt == maxAttempts.
approach:
Loop + Coroutine Delay

Loop through attempts. On success return early. On failure, if it's the last attempt rethrow. Otherwise compute delay = min(initialDelay × multiplier^(attempt-1), maxDelay), suspend with delay(), then continue.

What most candidates miss
  • Retrying on ALL exceptions — in production you'd filter: retry only on transient errors, not 4xx client errors
  • Not using minOf to cap the delay
  • Jitter — adding a small random offset to delays prevents thundering herd in distributed systems
summary: Retry a suspending call with exponential backoff using Kotlin coroutines. Android machine coding question with tests and a reference solution.

title: Shopping Cart with Discounts
description:
Problem

Design a Shopping Cart that supports multiple discount types using Kotlin's sealed classes.

Discount Types
  • PercentageOff — e.g. 20% off item price
  • FlatDiscount — e.g. ₹200 off the item
  • BuyXGetYFree — e.g. buy 2 get 1 free (pay for ceil(quantity / (buy+free) × buy) items)
Functional Requirements
  • addItem(item) — Add to cart or increase quantity if already present
  • removeItem(productId) — Remove item from cart
  • calculateTotal() — Return total price after all discounts
  • getAppliedDiscounts() — Return map of productId → discount amount saved
hints: Use a sealed class for Discount types. Each subtype carries different parameters — this is exactly what sealed classes are designed for.
In calculateTotal(), use a when expression on the Discount type for each item. For BuyXGetYFree: if you buy 3 with buy=2,free=1, you pay for 2.
For BuyXGetYFree: paidQuantity = ceil(quantity / (buyQuantity + freeQuantity).toFloat()) * buyQuantity
approach:
Sealed Class Dispatch

Use when (item.discount) in calculateTotal. Each branch handles its discount math. Store items in a MutableMap<String, CartItem> for O(1) add/update/remove by productId.

What most candidates miss
  • BuyXGetYFree calculation — most get the formula wrong for non-divisible quantities
  • Flat discount exceeding item price — should floor at 0, not go negative
  • Not handling duplicate addItem (should accumulate quantity, not replace)
summary: Model a shopping cart with sealed-class discounts in Kotlin. Android machine coding interview question with hints, tests and a solution.

title: In-Memory Cache with TTL
description:
Problem

Implement a generic in-memory cache with TTL (time-to-live) expiry for each entry.

Functional Requirements
  • put(key, value, ttlMs) — Store entry with an expiry time (defaults to defaultTtlMs)
  • get(key) — Return value if key exists and not expired, otherwise null
  • evictExpired() — Proactively remove all expired entries
  • size() — Return count of non-expired entries
Expiry Rule

An entry expires when currentTime >= insertionTime + ttlMs. Expired entries should not be returned by get even if not yet evicted.
hints: Store both the value and its expiry timestamp in a wrapper class.
Use a data class: CacheEntry(value: V, expiryAt: Long). Compute expiryAt = System.currentTimeMillis() + ttlMs at insertion time.
In get(), if entry exists but System.currentTimeMillis() >= entry.expiryAt, treat it as a miss (optionally remove it lazily). In size(), count only entries where expiryAt > currentTime.
approach:
Lazy Expiry + Proactive Eviction

Store Map<K, CacheEntry<V>> where each entry carries its absolute expiry timestamp. Lazy expiry on get — check and return null if expired. evictExpired() does a full sweep.

What most candidates miss
  • Thread safety — concurrent reads/writes need synchronization or ConcurrentHashMap
  • size() returning stale count — must filter expired entries
  • Not removing lazily-expired entries from the map (memory leak)
summary: Build a generic in-memory cache with per-entry TTL in Kotlin. Android machine coding interview question with hints, tests and a solution.

title: Order State Machine
description:
Problem

Implement a finite state machine for a food delivery order lifecycle using Kotlin sealed classes.

State Transitions
  • Placed → (Confirm) → Confirmed
  • Confirmed → (StartPreparing) → Preparing
  • Preparing → (Dispatch) → OutForDelivery
  • OutForDelivery → (MarkDelivered) → Delivered
  • Any state except Delivered → (Cancel) → Cancelled
Functional Requirements
  • transition(event) — Apply event, return true if valid, false if invalid for current state
  • getStatusDescription() — Return a human-readable status string
  • Invalid transitions must not change state
hints: Use sealed classes for both OrderState and OrderEvent. This gives exhaustive when expressions.
In transition(), use a when(currentState) outer block, then when(event) inner block. Any unmatched combination returns false.
The Cancel event is valid from most states — handle it in each non-terminal state's branch, or use an outer check before the main when block.
approach:
Sealed Class State Machine

Use nested when expressions. Outer: current state. Inner: incoming event. Only valid pairs update currentState and return true. Everything else returns false without mutating state.

What most candidates miss
  • Allowing Cancel from Delivered state — Delivered is terminal, nothing should transition out
  • Not returning false for unrecognised events — a default else clause matters
  • Missing the Cancelled → any transition (Cancelled is also terminal)
summary: Implement a food-order state machine with Kotlin sealed classes. Android machine coding interview question with hints, tests and a solution.

title: Restaurant Bill Screen
description:
Problem

Design and implement the restaurant bill screen below. Fetch bill data from a dummy API (simulated with a 1.5s delay), show a loading state, then render the check. This is a UI-focused machine coding challenge.

Target Screen
Toast
Burger$8.99
Fries$3.49
Soda$1.99
Ice Cream$1.99
Total:$15.67
Print
Pay $15.67
Header
  • Background: #FFFFFF · Padding: 12dp
  • "Toast" text — color #404040, size 16sp
Item List (RecyclerView)
  • Each row: item name (left) + price (right)
  • Scrollable — list length is dynamic from API
  • Show loading spinner while fetching
Footer
  • Background: #FFFFFF · Padding: 12dp
  • Total text — color #404040, size 16sp
  • Two buttons side by side · Height: 48dp
  • Margin top (from total): 8dp · Between buttons: 8dp
  • Button bg: #022CFA · Text: #FFFFFF, size 16sp
Dummy API — Mock this in your Repository
{
  "items": [
    { "name": "Burger",    "price": 8.99 },
    { "name": "Fries",     "price": 3.49 },
    { "name": "Soda",      "price": 1.99 },
    { "name": "Ice Cream", "price": 1.99 }
  ],
  "total": 15.67
}
// Simulate network latency: delay(1500) before emitting data

Requirements

  • Architecture: MVVM — ViewModel + Repository + sealed UiState
  • Use StateFlow in ViewModel, collect with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)
  • Use StateFlow.update { } — not .value =
  • Repository returns Flow<CheckData> with delay(1500)
  • Handle Loading → Success → Error states in the UI
  • Total amount and Pay button text must come from API data — do not hardcode
hints: Start with data models: data class CheckItem(val name: String, val price: Double) and CheckData(items, total). Then define a sealed CheckUiState with Loading, Success(data), Error(message).
Repository: fun getCheck(): Flow<CheckData> = flow { delay(1500); emit(mockData) }. ViewModel: private val _state = MutableStateFlow<CheckUiState>(Loading) — call .update{} never .value =.

In the Activity: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { vm.state.collect { when(it) { ... } } } }. On Loading → show ProgressBar, hide RecyclerView. On Success → reverse + call adapter.submitList() + update footer text.
Footer layout: parent LinearLayout with weightSum="2", each button layout_weight="1". Pay button text = "Pay $" + String.format("%.2f", total) — read from state, not hardcoded.
approach:
Architecture Flow

Repository flow { delay(1500); emit(data) } → ViewModel collects + maps to CheckUiState via MutableStateFlow.update{} → Activity collects with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) → UI renders per state.

Key Files

  • CheckItem.kt / CheckData.kt — data models
  • CheckUiState.kt — sealed class with Loading, Success, Error
  • CheckRepository.kt — interface + impl with Flow + delay(1500)
  • CheckViewModel.kt — MutableStateFlow + viewModelScope + .update{}
  • BillActivity.kt — repeatOnLifecycle + adapter + footer update
  • activity_bill.xml — header / FrameLayout(RecyclerView + ProgressBar) / footer
  • item_check_row.xml — two TextViews, horizontal LinearLayout
What most candidates miss
  • Using .value = instead of .update { } — not atomic
  • Collecting Flow in onCreate scope — leaks coroutine when app is backgrounded
  • Hardcoding "Pay $15.67" — interviewer WILL change the mock data to test this
  • Not handling Error state — ProgressBar keeps spinning if the API call fails
  • ProgressBar outside FrameLayout — it won't overlay the RecyclerView properly
summary: Build a restaurant bill screen on Android: Repository, StateFlow, ViewModel and RecyclerView. A UI machine coding interview challenge with hints.
